interactions.label: The clavicle is most commonly fractured at which site?

params.question: The clavicle is most commonly fractured at which site?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sternal end is the rounded medial end forming the sternoclavicular joint. It is not the weakest point. Fractures most commonly occur at the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third.

answers.text: Junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This junction is the weakest point of the clavicle. After fracture here, sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment upward while the arm's weight pulls the lateral fragment downward.
The flat acromial end forms the acromioclavicular joint laterally. The most common fracture site is at the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third — the thinnest part of the bone.

The subclavian groove is on the inferior surface and houses the subclavius muscle. The weakest point — and most common fracture site — is at the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third.

overallFeedback.feedback: The clavicle fractures most commonly at the junction of its medial two-thirds and lateral one-third — the weakest point. Sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment up; the arm's weight pulls the lateral fragment down.

Correct! The junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third is the weakest point. After fracture, sternocleidomastoid elevates the medial fragment while the arm's weight depresses the lateral fragment.

interactions.label: A mid-shaft fracture of the humerus is most likely to injure which nerve?

params.question: A mid-shaft fracture of the humerus is most likely to injure which nerve?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The axillary nerve is at risk at the surgical neck of the humerus (proximal end), not the mid-shaft. Surgical neck fractures endanger the axillary nerve, producing loss of deltoid function and shoulder abduction.
The ulnar nerve is vulnerable behind the medial epicondyle at the distal end of the humerus. Mid-shaft fractures endanger the radial nerve in the spiral groove, not the ulnar nerve.

The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis. It is not closely related to the humeral shaft. The radial nerve in the spiral groove is the nerve at risk here.
The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the posterior surface of the humeral mid-shaft. Its injury here produces wrist drop — inability to extend the wrist and fingers.

overallFeedback.feedback: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the posterior surface of the humeral shaft. A mid-shaft fracture here produces wrist drop. Remember: surgical neck → axillary nerve; mid-shaft → radial nerve; medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve.

Correct! The radial nerve travels in the spiral groove on the posterior humeral shaft. Mid-shaft fractures injure it, producing wrist drop — one of the most important nerve-fracture associations in anatomy.

params.question: What makes the scaphoid particularly vulnerable to avascular necrosis following fracture?

answers.text: It is the smallest bone in the proximal carpal row

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The scaphoid is actually the largest bone in the proximal carpal row, not the smallest. Its vulnerability to avascular necrosis comes from the extensive articular cartilage covering most of its surface, severely limiting blood vessel entry.

answers.text: It lies within the carpal tunnel, compressed by the flexor retinaculum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The scaphoid is in the proximal carpal row but does not lie within the carpal tunnel. Its avascular necrosis risk comes from articular cartilage covering most of its surface, restricting the points where blood vessels can enter.

answers.text: Most of its surface is covered by articular cartilage, limiting blood vessel entry

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Because articular cartilage covers most of the scaphoid, very few sites allow blood vessels to enter. A fracture across the waist can cut off supply to the proximal fragment, causing avascular necrosis.

answers.text: It forms a saddle joint that restricts collateral circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The saddle joint is formed by the trapezium with the first metacarpal, not the scaphoid. The scaphoid's vulnerability is due to articular cartilage covering most of its surface, leaving very few entry points for blood vessels.

overallFeedback.feedback: Most of the scaphoid's surface is articular cartilage, leaving very few points where blood vessels can enter. A fracture interrupts this already limited blood supply, and the proximal fragment can undergo avascular necrosis — explaining why early immobilisation is critical.

Correct! The extensive articular cartilage leaves very few entry points for blood vessels. A fracture — especially through the waist — can disrupt this limited supply, leading to avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment.
